A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work. Their text, equations, figures, tables and appendices support reliable comparison, including matching renamed generators and relocated synthetic experiments.

before.justification: v1 reports original synthetic experiments on CFE accuracy, dimensionality, action access, augmentation and prediction errors in Section 5, with dataset statistics in Appendix A.

after.justification: v2 retains original synthetic results and adds healthcare-derived experiments and recourse comparisons in Section 6 and Appendix D.

M1.justification: v2 adds signed continuous-action optimization under a linear classifier and extends learned action selection to these CFEs (Sections 3.1 and 4.1), beyond v1's binary capability/set-cover formulation. The original named, named-action and full-action learning approaches largely persist under revised terminology.

E1.justification: v1 evaluates fully synthetic capability-acquisition tasks. v2 additionally evaluates BMI and waist-to-hip-ratio recourse using NHANES and Foods data, and wellness-check recourse using BRFSS with synthetic actions. The original synthetic dimensionality, threshold and action-access scenarios remain.

E2.justification: v2 actually evaluates Ustun et al. (2019)'s low-level actionable recourse against high-level CFEs on healthcare-derived datasets (Section 6.1; Appendix D). v1 cites this work but does not report that comparison. The Hamming-distance baseline remains.

E3.justification: The added healthcare experiments introduce trained logistic classifiers, nutrient-specific actionability, monetary versus caloric objectives, and comparisons restricted to agents with both low- and high-level CFEs. New metrics include action counts, feature changes, state displacement and group variability. The original 80/20 split and zero-one accuracy metric are retained.

E4.justification: v2 adds demographic-group disparity analyses, correlations among recourse properties, cost-preference comparisons and healthcare case studies (Appendices D.1–D.2). Earlier dimensionality, frequency, action-access and augmentation analyses largely remain. The prediction-confidence histogram from v1 Figure 7(a) is removed.

E5.justification: v2 adds Kendall tau correlation tests and associated p-values (Section 6.1; Appendix C.2). The original accuracy-plus-margin reporting remains; neither PDF documents repeated-training-run counts or random seeds.

E6.justification: v2 adds healthcare accuracy and recourse-property results. For example, Table 1 reports 0.92 accuracy for hl-continuous generators on BMI and WHR, and 0.98 for hl-discrete generation on BRFSS, on the >40 datasets. These are new settings, not same-setting gains over v1. Most matched synthetic scores remain unchanged.

T1.justification: Definition 1 and Equation 2 in v2 extend the formal problem to signed, real-valued action effects constrained by a linear classifier. Equation 3 also adds the initial state xi to the set-cover coverage constraint, absent from v1 Section 2.1. These are substantive mathematical additions and corrections.

C1.justification: The abstract, contributions and conclusion broaden from learning optimal set-cover CFEs under information constraints to introducing high-level recourse types. v2 additionally claims fewer actions, greater agent improvement, fairer outcomes and interpretability advantages over low-level CFEs.

C2.justification: v2 introduces interpretations linking greater state displacement to agent improvement, lower group variability to fairness, and shared CFEs to scalability. It also qualifies cross-method cost comparability, discusses difficulty obtaining historical optimal-CFE data, and explicitly limits healthcare examples to illustrative use (Section 7; Appendix D).

D1.justification: v2 adds extensive healthcare preprocessing, feature-binarization and action-cost construction details, exact laptop specifications, and encoder-decoder settings. Its code link points to a different anonymous repository. Many dense-network hyperparameters were already documented in v1 and are retained.

R1.justification: v2 substantially repositions the contribution around high-level versus feature-based recourse, especially relative to Ustun et al. It adds discussion citing Barocas et al. (2020) and Verma et al. (2020), alongside dataset references, while retaining the earlier reinforcement-learning and data-driven algorithm-design connections.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction and results narrative are extensively rewritten around high-level recourse. Terminology changes throughout, related work moves to Section 8, limitations become Section 7, and most original synthetic results move into a substantially reorganized appendix.

P2.justification: v2 adds healthcare examples, comparison charts, correlation heatmaps and demographic-group plots, while relocating and restructuring existing displays. v1 Table 3 is split across v2 Tables 4 and 6. v2 Figure 19 also corrects the swapped neural-network/Hamming-distance panel labels in v1 Figure 6.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially addresses v1's synthetic-only validation and lack of direct comparison with feature-based recourse. Healthcare-derived action spaces, evaluated comparator results, subgroup analyses and detailed preprocessing materially strengthen empirical grounding and reproducibility. These gains outweigh the limitations of the stronger claims, particularly that fairness and agent improvement are assessed through group-variation and state-distance proxies rather than demonstrated real-world benefits.
